name: closures
intent: Create a function value together with the lexical environment it needs, so the function carries its own captured state with it and can be passed, stored and invoked long after the enclosing scope has exited.
problem: Behaviour that needs a handful of parameters must be handed the same configuration at every call site, or the configuration must live in mutable object fields - so the callback is coupled to the object that happens to hold the data, every entry point grows another parameter, and the 'hidden' state is invisible in the signature. Alternatively the behaviour has to be wrapped in a class whose only members are the captured values, which is the same state shipped with ceremony.
context: Applies where a small piece of behaviour is defined at the point where its inputs are already in scope - an event handler, a comparator for one call to sort, a validation rule for one field, a predicate for a query builder, a retry policy, a middleware - and is then handed to code that has no access to those variables and no business knowing their names. Also the standard way to give a value private mutable state without a class: a factory returns a function closing over locals that nothing else can name. The decision is whether the environment travels by capture or by explicit argument list, and whether capture is by reference or by value.
benefits: The captured configuration travels inside the function value, so the function is self-describing: its type is just a function type and its dependencies are not extra parameters that every call site must supply.
Private state without a class: a factory function's locals cannot be read or written from outside, so a counter, a cache or an accumulator can be owned by the closure rather than exposed as fields.

Deferred binding removes temporal coupling - the handler can be created before the event that will trigger it occurs, and invoked from a dispatcher that knows nothing about the scope it was written in.
Comparators, predicates and key functions become one-liners at the call site: sort(data, f(a, b)), filter(xs, p(x)), map(xs, g(x)) need no named class when the rule is only three lines long.
Callbacks and listeners close naturally over loop state, so the common 'register ten handlers, each with its own index' case needs no explicit capture object.
Continuations, decorators, memoization and state machines are all built from closures, so knowing capture makes the advanced functional idioms readable rather than magical.
tradeoffs: The captured environment is invisible in the signature, so a reader cannot see what a handler depends on; tooling that cannot introspect closures - profilers, serializers, dependency injectors, most ORMs - treats the value as opaque.

Capture by reference aliases the enclosing variable: every closure over it observes later mutations, so a loop that keeps appending handlers often captures the final value of the loop variable and produces ten identical callbacks.

A long-lived closure pins every variable it captured, including large intermediates, and the retention lasts as long as the closure is reachable - a classic memory leak shape in long-lived listeners and global registries.
Escape analysis decides whether a closure allocates; one that outlives the frame is a heap object, so closure-heavy inner loops can allocate per iteration and erase the abstraction's benefit.
Per-instance allocation: a closure created inside a constructor or a frequently-called method allocates one object per instance or per call where a plain virtual method would allocate nothing.

Naming and readability degrade when capture stands in for an explicit design: 'callback' functions taking four implicitly captured arguments read as though they took none, and the flow of data has to be reconstructed by hand.
Deep chains of closures that call closures are hard to profile and hard to debug - the stack shows only the current frame, not which closure instance produced it.
quality_attributes_note: Coupling scores low because capture removes the dependency from the signature - the coupling still exists, it is just not written down. Observability is low for the same reason: a closure is opaque to profilers and serializers, and the captured environment is invisible at the call site.

participants.responsibility: The compiled body of the function, shared by every closure created from the same definition.
participants.notes: The pointer is the cheap part; all instances of one lambda share it.

participants.responsibility: The subset of the enclosing frame's variables the body actually references, stored with the code pointer and kept alive for the closure's lifetime.
participants.notes: Implementations store either the whole enclosing frame (naive) or only the referenced slots (optimised, via closure conversion).

participants.responsibility: The pair (code, environment) as a first-class value: assignable, passable, storable in a container, comparable by identity.
participants.notes: This is the value the pattern actually produces.

participants.responsibility: Builds the environment at the point where the captured variables are in scope and live, then binds them into the closure.
participants.notes: Its locals become private state; nothing outside can name them.

participants.responsibility: Invokes the closure later, from an arbitrary point, with no knowledge of or access to the captured environment.

use_cases: Event and UI callbacks that close over the widget, connection or request they belong to, as in every JavaScript addEventListener and Python functools-style handler.
Sorting, grouping and querying with a one-use comparator or predicate: sort(rows, key=lambda r: r.deadline), sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e.weight).
Private state without a class: a makeCounter() factory returning a closure over an integer is the canonical textbook form and appears in real caches and rate limiters.
Deferred configuration in middleware chains and retry loops, where the policy is built where the settings are known and applied where the failures occur.
Memoization decorators, which capture the target function plus a cache keyed by its arguments.
Test doubles: a stub that records calls to a dependency is a closure over a list, and needs no class, mocking framework or generated code.
Registration tables: building a map of handler closures keyed by message type in one pass, replacing a dispatch switch and a family of near-identical methods.
avoid_when: The handler outlives the data it captures and is registered globally or in a long-lived listener list - promote the state to an explicit field or a weak-reference-keyed registry.
The captured set is large or the closure is created per element in a hot loop; a struct with two fields and a virtual method allocates the same way and reads better in a profiler.
The value must be serialised, compared structurally, reflected over or injected - most such frameworks cannot see through a closure, so use a named type.
Five or more values are captured: at that point the function has a hidden parameter list and an explicit signature is the more honest interface.

The language's capture semantics are surprising (loop variables shared across iterations, capture by reference where value was meant) and the code must be provably correct rather than probably correct.
Ordinary control flow needs no deferral - a helper function with parameters is faster, debuggable and stack-traceable.
pitfalls: Late binding in loops: creating handlers inside a for loop with a mutable loop variable makes every closure see the final value. Capture per iteration explicitly (Python's default argument trick, Java's for-each binding, a factory call) or use a language whose loop variable is per-iteration.

Capture by reference in C++: a lambda storing a reference to a local outliving the function dangles. Use value capture for by-value locals, and if the state must be shared use a smart pointer deliberately.

Retain cycles: an object holding a closure that captures the object is a cycle; in a tracing collector it leaks, and in a reference-counted runtime it never runs its destructor. Break the cycle with weak references.
Allocation per call in a hot path: a closure created inside a frequently invoked function is a heap object unless the compiler proves it does not escape; hoist it or use a stateless function object.
Opaque to tooling: debuggers, JSON serializers and DI containers cannot introspect the environment, so the hidden dependencies never appear in documentation or error messages.

Indirection defeating optimisation: a megamorphic call site that sees many closure types cannot be inlined or specialised, so a hot path that was monomorphic becomes slow purely because closures were used.

Mutating captured state under concurrency: two threads invoking the same counter closure race on the captured variable unless the language serialises it; the capture hides the shared mutable state that a reviewer would otherwise spot.

related_patterns_notes.function-composition: Closures are the currency; composition is what you build from them. Composition is a closure of closures - f.andThen(g) captures f and g and returns a new callable - so it presupposes capture.
related_patterns_notes.currying-partial-application: Both bind arguments to a function value, but partial application fixes the *leading* arguments as ordinary values while a closure fixes them as a *capture site*: the captured variables remain live and may change between invocations, which is the difference between a closure and a specialised function.
related_patterns_notes.method-object: Both give behaviour access to a fixed set of state. Method-object is the OO answer (an object holding the function and its collaborators, visible to tooling); the closure is the functional answer, with the same reachability expressed invisibly.
related_patterns_notes.memoization: A memoizing decorator is implemented by capturing the wrapped function in a cache closure; the cache is private state that only the closure can name.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: In Python a decorator is a closure factory by construction: def deco(fn) returns a wrapper closing over fn.
related_patterns_notes.higher-order-component: The React-specific special case where the captured 'environment' is other components, so the enhancer is a closure over components.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter-as-data: Closures are the representation defunctionalisation removes: an interpreter written in CPS and then defunctionalised replaces the function values with a finite sum type, which is the explicit form of what closures encode implicitly.
related_patterns_notes.identity-function: The degenerate closure: a function that captures nothing. It is the identity element of the composition monoid and the correct choice whenever a function value is required but no state is captured.

anti_patterns: The loop-variable capture bug: registering handlers in a loop without per-iteration binding, so every callback fires with the same index.
The global registry: adding a closure to a module-level list or a long-lived observer and never removing it, leaking the entire captured environment.
Capture as an excuse for a missing parameter: a function whose real inputs are four implicit captures cannot be called correctly from any other context.
Deeply nested closure factories - a closure returned from a closure returned from a factory - that turn simple control flow into an unreadable chain of environments.
Using a closure where the language's virtual dispatch is clearer and cheaper: one allocation per object for state that two fields would hold inline.
Capturing 'self' in an event handler registered on the object itself, creating a cycle that keeps the object and everything it points at alive.
Serializing a closure: passing a lambda to a queue, a config file or a remote worker, where only a named, introspectable value survives.
design_principles: Bind late: the value of a closure is that the binding happens where the values are in scope, not that it happens early.
Smallest sufficient mechanism: capture is for a handful of values; beyond that the dependency list belongs in the signature.
Reachability rules lifetime: whatever a closure captures stays alive as long as the closure does - treat the environment as part of the closure's footprint.
Explicit is better than captured when the value must be observed: names in a signature can be seen, counted and tested.
best_practices: Keep the captured set small - if you are capturing more than about four things, introduce a parameter object or a small struct.
Bind loop variables per iteration explicitly when the language shares them, and add a test that fires each registered handler and asserts distinct arguments.
Prefer value capture over reference capture unless sharing is intended; a reference to a local outliving its scope is a dangling pointer, not a fast path.
Use weak references for long-lived registrations so the closure does not pin the object it observes.
Hoist closures out of hot loops: create the function once at module or object level when it captures nothing that varies per iteration.
Give captured state a name in a comment when it is non-obvious, since no signature will carry it.
Favour a stateless named function when the captured values are known at import time - it is faster, serializable and visible in a stack trace.
Add a lifetime budget test for long-lived listeners: create, fire, release, and assert the captured objects are collected.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Closure (computer programming)' - the canonical definition of a closure as a function paired with its lexical environment, Landin's origin, and the capture-by-value vs capture-by-reference split. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(computer_science)

Xavier Leroy, 'Functional programming languages - Part III: program transformations' (typing course, Radboud University) - closure conversion defined as the transformation that makes environment construction explicit, with the free-variable formula. http://cs.ru.nl/~freek/courses/tt-2017/papers/transformations.pdf

Olivier Danvy, 'Defunctionalization at Work' (TOPLAS) - explains why closures are the standard representation of first-class functions and how closure conversion relates to defunctionalization. https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/olivier-danvy/defunc.pdf

Wikipedia, 'Closure (computer programming)' - the Smalltalk observation that all of Smalltalk's control structures are defined with objects whose methods accept closures, i.e. closures as a control-structure primitive rather than a callback convenience. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(computer_science)
